text: An elephant's trunk joins its nose and upper lip into a flexible muscular organ. It can manipulate food, draw in water, explore by touch, and carry odors to the nose.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: An Asian elephant has a single fingerlike projection at the tip of its trunk, useful for precise grasping.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: An elephant's ears contain many blood vessels. Flapping them helps transfer heat from circulating blood to the air.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Elephants walk on their toes, with thick fibrous pads beneath their feet cushioning the load.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: An elephant's molars are replaced from behind as worn teeth move forward. Tooth wear and replacement give clues to the animal's age.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Elephants use low-frequency rumbles for communication over long distances; some of this sound lies below ordinary human hearing.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, Asian elephant fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/asian-elephant. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A fennec fox's oversized ears serve two tasks: shedding heat and locating prey beneath sand.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, fennec fox fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/fennec-fox. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Fur on a fennec fox's paws helps with traction in sand and shields the feet from hot ground.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, fennec fox fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/fennec-fox. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Fennec foxes hunt at night and shelter in burrows during the hottest daylight hours. A den can have multiple entrances.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, fennec fox fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/fennec-fox. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Fennec foxes obtain water from their food and can go for extended periods without drinking.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, fennec fox fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/fennec-fox. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A giant panda grips bamboo with a fleshy pad supported by an enlarged wrist bone: a pseudo-thumb rather than a true extra digit.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, giant panda fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/giant-panda. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A giant panda's digestive tract retains features of its carnivorous ancestry. Inefficient extraction of nutrients from bamboo makes long feeding periods necessary.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, giant panda fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/giant-panda. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Giant pandas leave scent marks on rocks, ground, and tree trunks. The marks carry social information even when the animals are far apart.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, giant panda fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/giant-panda. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Iron in a beaver's tooth enamel contributes to its orange color and strengthens the outer surface. The incisors grow continuously and are worn down by use.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, beaver fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/beaver. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A beaver's hind foot has a specialized double toenail used to comb its fur, helping preserve insulation and waterproofing.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, beaver fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/beaver. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A beaver can draw a transparent membrane over its eyes while underwater. Its ears also close during submersion.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, beaver fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/beaver. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A beaver's flattened tail helps steer during swimming and brace the body on land. A slap on the water can signal danger.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, beaver fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/beaver. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Beaver dams slow water and create ponds. The change in flow produces habitat used by many other species.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, beaver fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/beaver. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Orangutans usually move through trees by careful climbing and walking, distributing their weight among branches. Their long arms and grasping feet suit this arboreal travel.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, orangutan fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/orangutan. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A male orangutan's long call resonates in an enlarged throat sac. It advertises his presence across the forest.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, orangutan fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/orangutan. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Some orangutan vocalizations occur in particular wild populations and are absent in others; the Smithsonian describes these differences as cultural.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, orangutan fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/orangutan. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: A lion pride is built around related females and their offspring, with one or more resident males. Members often associate in smaller subgroups.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, lion fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/lion. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Young male lions may form coalitions with brothers or cousins after leaving their natal pride.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, lion fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/lion. Consulted 2026-10-13.

text: Several lions may approach prey from different directions before attacking. Females are the primary hunters in a pride, though males sometimes join.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Source: Smithsonian National Zoo, lion fact sheet; https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/lion. Consulted 2026-10-13.
